patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Found sweaty, confused and slurring his words by his wife at 7 am
background: Type 2 diabetes for 12 years on metformin and gliclazide
Chronic kidney disease stage 3; diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days, barely eating
One severe hypo needing paramedics 4 months ago
Retired bus driver from Lewisham; still drives his own car

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'Which medication is the most likely cause?' with a confused, sweaty diabetic on insulin or a sulphonylurea and a capillary glucose below 4.0 mmol/L.

points: Desmond, 67, type 2 diabetes on **gliclazide** and metformin.
Three days of diarrhoea and vomiting; hardly eating, still taking his tablets.
Wife found him **drenched in sweat**, shaking and talking nonsense.
Paramedics bring him in; he is drowsy but rousable.

steps.lead: A confused, sweaty diabetic is hypoglycaemic until a finger-prick says otherwise. The cut-off to remember is **below 4.0 mmol/L**.

visual.title: Capillary blood glucose
visual.label: Desmond 2.1
visual.caption: Desmond is well below 4.0 mmol/L and below 3.0, where severe neuroglycopenic symptoms appear.

steps.text: The paramedics' finger-prick glucose is the single most important number in the case.

steps.lead: Desmond has the classic set-up: a **sulphonylurea** plus **missed meals** from his gastroenteritis.

points: Speech slurred; does not know where he is.
No focal limb weakness; pupils equal and reactive.
No smell of ketones, not dehydrated-looking enough for HHS.

steps.q: Which of Desmond's features is neuroglycopenic rather than autonomic?
steps.r: **Slurred speech** reflects the brain running out of glucose. Sweating, tremor and palpitations are the **adrenaline** warning signs.

steps.lead: Desmond has both sets: autonomic (sweating, tremor, palpitations) and neuroglycopenic (**confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness**).
Desmond's cause is his drug, but **Whipple's triad** still applies: symptoms, a low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is given. In a non-diabetic, think **insulinoma**.

steps.text: A drowsy patient with slurred speech can look like a **stroke**. Always check the **capillary glucose** first; hypoglycaemia can even cause focal signs.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (capillary glucose) or a C-peptide question: raised means endogenous insulin (insulinoma, sulphonylurea), low means injected insulin.

steps.q: Desmond arrives confused and sweaty. Which test comes first?
steps.r: A **finger-prick glucose** takes seconds and changes management immediately. Do it before any scan.

steps.lead: Desmond's finger-prick reads 2.1 mmol/L; a **laboratory glucose** sent at the same time confirms it.

steps.title: Bloods taken before treatment
steps.text: AKI on CKD means gliclazide is not being cleared. Raised C-peptide fits drug-driven endogenous insulin.

visual.title: Desmond's kidney function
visual.label: Desmond 26
visual.caption: Dehydration pushed his eGFR down, so the sulphonylurea built up and kept driving insulin release.

steps.lead: Desmond's **C-peptide is raised**: his own pancreas is over-secreting insulin, as expected with a sulphonylurea. Injected insulin would give a **low** C-peptide.

steps.title: Reading the C-peptide
nodes: Send insulin and C-peptide at the time of the low
C-peptide low with high insulin → exogenous insulin
steps.caption: C-peptide is cut from proinsulin in the beta cell, so it only comes with the body's own insulin.

steps.text: Suspected **insulinoma** in a non-diabetic: the diagnostic test is a **72-hour supervised fast**, with insulin, proinsulin and ketones taken at the moment glucose drops.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where consciousness decides: oral glucose if able to swallow, buccal gel if conscious but not able to self-treat, IV glucose if GCS below 15, IM glucagon if no IV access.

steps.title: Treatment by conscious level
nodes: Conscious, can swallow → oral fast-acting glucose
GCS <15 or seizing → IV glucose over 10 min
steps.caption: Recheck the capillary glucose after each step.

steps.q: Desmond's GCS is 13 and he has a cannula. What do you give?
steps.r: GCS below 15 is not safe for oral treatment. With **IV access**, give **100 ml of 20%** (or 200 ml of 10%) glucose over 10 minutes.

steps.lead: Had Desmond been fully alert, **oral fast-acting glucose** would do. If alert but unable to self-treat, **buccal Glucogel**.
Desmond gets **100 ml of 20% glucose IV**, then toast and a sandwich once he can swallow safely. With no cannula, IM glucagon.

visual.title: Desmond's glucose after treatment
visual.caption: Gliclazide outlasts the IV glucose: the dip at 4 hours is why sulphonylurea hypos are admitted and monitored.

steps.text: Do not send a sulphonylurea hypo home after one good reading. The drug has a long action, worse in **renal impairment**, so hypoglycaemia recurs.

points: Gliclazide stopped while his kidneys recover; diabetes team reviews his drugs.
This is his **second severe hypo this year**, both while awake.
He plans to drive himself home from the ward.

steps.lead: Desmond needs a **medication and diet review**, and two severe episodes while awake mean he must **stop driving** and tell the DVLA.
Desmond's discharge plan follows **DVLA** guidance on severe hypoglycaemia; **Whipple's triad** is the rule for proving a hypo caused the symptoms.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why sweating comes before confusion, why awareness is lost, or how a sulphonylurea causes hypoglycaemia.

steps.lead: Desmond's sweating and tremor were **adrenaline**: the body's counter-regulatory alarm as glucose fell.
His confusion came later, once the **glucose-dependent brain** ran short of fuel.

steps.title: From falling glucose to coma
nodes: Glucose keeps falling: brain fuel runs out
steps.caption: Autonomic warning signs normally come first.

steps.lead: Desmond still gets warning sweats. Repeated hypos can blunt this response, so patients go straight to **unheralded** confusion.

steps.q: How does gliclazide cause Desmond's hypoglycaemia?
o: Blocks beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels, releasing insulin
Inhibits hepatic glucose output via AMPK
steps.r: Sulphonylureas close **K-ATP channels**, depolarising the beta cell so it releases insulin whatever the glucose level.

steps.lead: Desmond's own insulin, released by gliclazide, kept pushing glucose into cells and switching off **hepatic glucose output** while he was not eating.

steps.text: **Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia** because it does not raise insulin. In a stem with both drugs, the sulphonylurea is the culprit.

mcq.q: Below which blood glucose is hypoglycaemia clinically significant?
mcq.r: Clinically significant hypoglycaemia is **below 4.0 mmol/L**; severe symptoms often appear below 3.0.

mcq.q: Which is an autonomic feature of hypoglycaemia?
mcq.r: **Sweating**, tremor, palpitations and anxiety are autonomic; the rest are neuroglycopenic.

mcq.q: Which oral diabetes drug class most often causes hypoglycaemia?
mcq.r: **Sulphonylureas** (e.g. gliclazide) stimulate insulin release regardless of glucose.

o: Symptoms, low glucose at the time, relief with glucose
Weight gain, fasting symptoms, raised insulin
mcq.r: **Symptoms + a low glucose at the time + resolution with glucose**: classically used for insulinoma.

mcq.q: What does a low C-peptide with high insulin suggest?
mcq.r: Injected insulin has no C-peptide, so C-peptide is **not raised** with **exogenous insulin**.

mcq.q: What is the diagnostic test for insulinoma?
mcq.r: A **72-hour supervised fast**, with a hormone profile taken at the moment of hypoglycaemia.

mcq.q: Unconscious hypoglycaemia, no IV access. What do you give?
mcq.r: **IM glucagon** when IV glucose cannot be given; nothing by mouth if unconscious.

mcq.q: Which IV glucose regimen is used for severe hypoglycaemia?
mcq.r: **100 ml of 20%** or 200 ml of 10% glucose over about 10 minutes.

mcq.q: After how many severe hypos while awake must a driver stop and tell the DVLA?
mcq.r: **More than one** severe episode while awake, or **one while driving**.

mcq.q: Why do autonomic symptoms usually come before confusion?
o: Adrenaline is released as glucose falls
mcq.r: The **counter-regulatory sympathetic response** fires first, a warning before brain fuel runs out.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man with type 1 diabetes is found by his flatmate sweating and confused after a night out drinking. He played football earlier that day and took his usual insulin. He is tremulous, his speech is slurred and he cannot say where he is. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. There is no focal neurological deficit.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a confused diabetic: the drug, the timing and the skin decide it.
Insulin plus exercise plus alcohol all lower glucose. **Sweating and tremor** are autonomic; confusion is neuroglycopenic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Usual insulin dose after exercise and alcohol: **hypoglycaemia**. Check a capillary glucose.

elim: Alcohol does not explain the sweating and tremor; never blame drink before checking glucose.
DKA builds over hours with vomiting and dry skin, not sweating, and follows missed insulin.
No fever, headache or neck stiffness.
No head injury history and no focal signs.

steps.x: **C. Hypoglycaemia.** Rule: sweaty + confused + insulin = check the glucose first.

technique.stem: A 45 year old nurse without diabetes has had three episodes of sweating and confusion at work in a month. During the latest episode her capillary glucose was 2.2 mmol/L and her symptoms resolved with oral glucose. Bloods were sent at the time.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish an endogenous from an exogenous cause?

steps.x: It asks to separate **endogenous** (own insulin) from **exogenous** (injected) insulin.
Whipple's triad is met. A nurse has access to insulin, so exogenous insulin is on the list.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **C-peptide**: raised with own insulin (insulinoma, sulphonylurea), low with injected insulin.

elim: The supervised fast diagnoses insulinoma but does not answer the endogenous vs exogenous question first.
Imaging comes after a biochemical diagnosis of insulinoma.
HbA1c measures average glucose, not insulin source.
Synacthen tests for adrenal insufficiency; insulin would not be high.

steps.x: **D. Serum C-peptide.** Rule: C-peptide travels only with the body's own insulin.

technique.stem: A 71 year old woman with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide is brought to the emergency department after her carer found her drowsy. She opens her eyes to voice and is confused. Her GCS is 12. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. Her capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L. A cannula has been sited.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of hypoglycaemia: consciousness and IV access decide the route.
GCS below 15 rules out anything by mouth. IV access is available.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV glucose**: 100 ml of 20% (or 200 ml of 10%) over 10 minutes.

elim: Buccal gel is for a conscious patient who cannot self-treat.
IM glucagon is only if there is no IV access; it also works less well with sulphonylureas.
Oral glucose risks aspiration with a GCS of 12.
Long-acting carbohydrate comes after the glucose is corrected.

steps.x: **C. IV 20% glucose.** Rule: GCS <15 with a cannula = IV glucose; no cannula = IM glucagon.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 20 years has had two episodes of being found unconscious with a capillary glucose below 2.5 mmol/L. She says she no longer gets the shaky, sweaty feeling she used to have before a hypo. She has had many mild hypos this year.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her loss of warning symptoms?

steps.x: A mechanism question: why have the warning signs gone?

clues: no longer gets the shaky, sweaty feeling
steps.x: The lost symptoms are the **autonomic** ones. Repeated hypos and long-standing diabetes blunt them.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness**: a blunted sympathetic (adrenaline) warning response, from autonomic neuropathy.

elim: This would explain less brain fuel shortage, not lost sweating and tremor.
Antibodies cause erratic glucose, not loss of warning symptoms.
This makes hypos more likely but does not remove the warning signs.
Explains more hypos (e.g. renal failure), not unawareness.

steps.x: **A. Blunted autonomic response.** Rule: lost sweats and tremor = impaired awareness, so hypos go straight to coma.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department by her boyfriend. She skipped lunch after her usual morning insulin and went to the gym. She is anxious, sweaty and shaking, and keeps repeating herself. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 124/72 mmHg and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Insulin, a missed meal and exercise with sweating, tremor and confusion is hypoglycaemia. An anxiety attack also gives autonomic symptoms but not confusion.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a type 1 diabetic: think of the three diabetic emergencies.

clues: skipped lunch after her usual morning insulin
steps.x: Insulin with no food and extra exercise. Autonomic plus neuroglycopenic symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypoglycaemia**.

elim: Addisonian crisis gives hypotension and vomiting; no steroid history here.
Anxiety gives autonomic symptoms but not confusion; never diagnose it in an insulin user without a glucose.
DKA follows missed insulin and gives vomiting, dehydration and Kussmaul breathing.
HHS is a type 2 condition developing over days.

steps.x: **E. Hypoglycaemia.** Insulin + missed meal + exercise = hypo.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in confused. He has had a urinary tract infection and has been drinking little for 4 days. His medications are atorvastatin, bendroflumethiazide, gliclazide, metformin and ramipril. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which of his medications is the most likely cause of his hypoglycaemia?
practice.e: Gliclazide stimulates insulin release and accumulates when the kidneys fail. Metformin does not raise insulin and rarely causes hypoglycaemia on its own.

steps.x: Most likely cause from a drug list: find the drug that raises insulin.
Poor intake, AKI and a sulphonylurea: the classic accumulation set-up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gliclazide**, a sulphonylurea.

elim: Statins do not lower glucose.
Thiazides tend to raise glucose.
Metformin causes lactic acidosis in AKI, not hypoglycaemia.
ACE inhibitors worsen AKI but do not directly cause hypos.

steps.x: **C. Gliclazide.** Rule: hypo + AKI + sulphonylurea = the sulphonylurea.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman without diabetes has a 6 month history of episodes of sweating, palpitations and confusion, usually before breakfast or after missing meals. The episodes stop when she eats. She has gained 7 kg because she eats frequently to prevent them. During one episode her capillary glucose was 2.3 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fasting hypoglycaemia with Whipple's triad and weight gain in a non-diabetic is insulinoma. Dumping syndrome gives post-prandial symptoms after gastric surgery.

steps.x: Diagnosis of recurrent hypoglycaemia in someone not on diabetes drugs.

clues: before breakfast or after missing meals
steps.x: Symptoms, a low glucose at the time and relief with food: **Whipple's triad**. Fasting pattern and weight gain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Insulinoma**, a functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour.

elim: Addison's gives weight loss, pigmentation and hypotension.
Dumping is after meals and after gastric surgery.
Phaeochromocytoma gives paroxysmal hypertension with high, not low, glucose.
Vasovagal syncope is brief and has a normal glucose.

steps.x: **C. Insulinoma.** Rule: Whipple's triad in a non-diabetic = insulinoma until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 22 years is brought in after being found unconscious at work. His capillary glucose was 1.8 mmol/L and he recovered with IV glucose. He says he no longer feels sweaty or shaky before a hypo, which he used to. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his lack of warning symptoms?
practice.e: Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness is due to autonomic neuropathy blunting the sympathetic warning response. Peripheral sensory neuropathy affects the feet, not the adrenaline response.

steps.x: Most likely cause of losing hypo warning signs.

clues: no longer feels sweaty or shaky
steps.x: Long-standing diabetes; the autonomic warning symptoms have gone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autonomic neuropathy** causing impaired hypoglycaemia awareness.

elim: Retinopathy affects vision, not hypo awareness.
Hypothyroidism does not remove sweating and tremor.
Sensory neuropathy affects feeling in the feet, not the sympathetic response.
Myopathy causes weakness, not unawareness.

steps.x: **A. Autonomic neuropathy.** Rule: lost warning signs = impaired awareness.

practice.stem: A baby boy born at 34 weeks' gestation is 6 hours old. The midwife notices he is jittery, feeding poorly and sweaty. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 168 bpm. There is no rash and the fontanelle is soft.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Prematurity is a specific risk factor for neonatal hypoglycaemia, and the glucose is low with normal calcium and CRP. Hypocalcaemia also causes jitteriness but the calcium is normal.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a jittery newborn: check the labs for the cause.
Preterm (<37 weeks) is a risk factor. In the bloods, glucose is low; calcium and CRP are normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neonatal hypoglycaemia**.

elim: HIE follows a difficult delivery with low Apgars; none is described.
No maternal opiate history and symptoms usually start later.
Calcium is normal.
No fever, normal CRP.

steps.x: **D. Neonatal hypoglycaemia.** Prematurity is the risk factor to spot.

practice.stem: A 29 year old healthcare assistant without diabetes is brought to the emergency department confused and sweating. Her capillary glucose is 1.7 mmol/L and she recovers with IV glucose. Her sister has type 1 diabetes. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Bloods were taken before treatment.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypoglycaemia?
practice.e: High insulin with low C-peptide means the insulin was injected. Insulinoma and sulphonylureas both raise C-peptide.

steps.x: Cause of hypoglycaemia: read the insulin and C-peptide together.
Access to insulin. In the bloods: very high insulin but undetectable C-peptide.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Exogenous insulin**: injected insulin carries no C-peptide.

elim: Alcohol suppresses gluconeogenesis but insulin would be low.
Insulinoma makes insulin and C-peptide together, so C-peptide is raised.
Non-islet tumours act via IGF-2 with low insulin.
Sulphonylureas raise C-peptide and the screen is negative.

steps.x: **B. Exogenous insulin.** Rule: high insulin + low C-peptide = injected.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin is brought in by ambulance after his wife found him drowsy and sweating. He mumbles but does not answer questions. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There is no focal weakness.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: A capillary (finger-prick) glucose is fast and changes treatment immediately. CT head is for when glucose is normal and a stroke or head injury is suspected.

steps.x: Initial investigation: the quickest test that changes management.
Insulin user, sweaty and drowsy: hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Finger-prick capillary glucose**.

elim: Scan only after glucose is checked and corrected.
C-peptide finds the cause later; it is not the first test.
Toxicology is not the first step in a sweaty insulin user.
A gas is useful for DKA, but glucose comes first and is quicker.

steps.x: **A. Capillary blood glucose.** Rule: check the glucose in anyone with reduced consciousness, before any scan.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman without diabetes has recurrent fasting episodes of confusion that resolve with food. During an episode her plasma glucose was 2.0 mmol/L with a raised insulin and raised C-peptide. A sulphonylurea screen was negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Suspected insulinoma is diagnosed by a 72-hour supervised fast with a hormone profile at the time of hypoglycaemia. An OGTT tests for diabetes, not fasting hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for endogenous hyperinsulinism.
Endogenous insulin, no drug: insulinoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **72-hour supervised fast**.

elim: HbA1c reflects average glucose, not insulin excess.
OGTT diagnoses diabetes and provokes post-prandial, not fasting, responses.
Cortisol screens adrenal failure, which would not raise insulin.
Synacthen tests adrenal reserve, not insulinoma.

steps.x: **A. 72-hour supervised fast.** Rule: proven endogenous hyperinsulinism, no drug = supervised fast.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide feels shaky and sweaty in the clinic waiting room. He is fully alert, talking normally and able to swallow. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Conscious and able to swallow: oral fast-acting glucose such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink, followed by a longer-acting carbohydrate. IV and IM routes are for reduced consciousness.

steps.x: Initial management: how conscious is he?
Hypoglycaemic but alert and safe to swallow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral fast-acting glucose** (tablets, Lucozade, orange juice).

elim: Buccal gel is for a conscious patient unable to self-treat.
Glucagon is for the unconscious with no IV access.
IV glucose is for GCS below 15 or seizures.
A slow snack alone is too slow; it follows fast glucose.

steps.x: **D. Oral fast-acting glucose.** Then a longer-acting carbohydrate.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is found having a seizure in a park. A friend says she injected insulin and skipped lunch. The paramedic's capillary glucose is 1.5 mmol/L. Two attempts at IV access have failed. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 140/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: A seizing hypoglycaemic patient with no IV access needs IM glucagon. Nothing should go in the mouth during a seizure.

steps.x: Initial management: conscious level and IV access decide.

clues: Two attempts at IV access have failed
steps.x: Seizing, severe hypo, no IV route.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IM glucagon**.

elim: Nothing by mouth in a seizing patient; gel is for conscious patients.
IV access has failed.
Aspiration risk.
The seizure is from hypoglycaemia; treat the cause.

steps.x: **B. IM glucagon.** Rule: unconscious or seizing with no IV = IM glucagon.

practice.stem: A 54 year old taxi driver with type 2 diabetes on insulin is reviewed in clinic. He has had two episodes this year where his wife needed to give him glucose because he was too confused to treat himself, both at home while awake. He has not had a hypo while driving. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?
o: Check glucose before each journey and continue driving
Continue driving and inform the DVLA only after a third episode
Stop driving for 24 hours after each episode
Stop driving immediately and inform the DVLA
practice.e: More than one severe hypo (needing help from another person) while awake means he must stop driving and inform the DVLA. Checking glucose before driving is good practice but does not replace this.

steps.x: DVLA question: count the severe episodes and where they happened.
Severe = needs help from another person. Two while awake.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop driving and inform the DVLA**.

elim: Pre-drive checks do not override the DVLA rule.
The threshold is more than one, which he has already met.
There is no 24-hour rule for this.
Time of day is irrelevant.

steps.x: **D. Stop driving and inform the DVLA.** Rule: >1 severe while awake, or 1 while driving.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes develops recurrent hypoglycaemia after starting a new tablet. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. His serum C-peptide is raised during an episode. The tablet is a sulphonylurea.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Blocks ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells
Inhibits SGLT2 in the proximal tubule
practice.e: Sulphonylureas close K-ATP channels on beta cells, causing depolarisation and insulin release regardless of glucose, which explains the raised C-peptide. AMPK activation is metformin.

steps.x: Mechanism of a sulphonylurea.
Raised C-peptide means the drug drives the patient's own insulin release.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Closes beta-cell K-ATP channels** → depolarisation → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin release.

elim: PPAR-gamma is pioglitazone; it improves sensitivity.
DPP-4 inhibitors raise incretins in a glucose-dependent way.
AMPK is metformin; it does not raise insulin.
SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria, rarely hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: **B. Blocks K-ATP channels.** Insulin release whatever the glucose = hypo risk.

prompts.q: Define hypoglycaemia and name its two groups of symptoms, with examples.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you a mix of symptoms; sort them into the two groups.

points.p: Blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L
points.why: Severe symptoms often appear below 3.0 mmol/L.

points.p: Autonomic: sweating, tremor, palpitations, anxiety
points.why: These come from adrenaline and usually come first.

points.p: Neuroglycopenic: confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech, seizures, coma
points.why: These reflect the brain running out of glucose.

prompts.q: Who gets hypoglycaemia? Name the main causes and risk factors.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: find the drug in the stem, then the reason it tipped over.

points.p: Diabetes treated with insulin
points.why: The most important cause.

points.p: Sulphonylureas such as gliclazide
points.why: Metformin alone rarely causes hypos.

points.p: Missed meals (plus exercise, alcohol)
points.why: Usual dose with less food is the classic precipitant.

points.p: Impaired awareness from autonomic neuropathy
points.why: These patients go straight to confusion without warning.

points.p: Neonates: prematurity (<37 weeks)
points.why: The specific neonatal risk factor in the notes.

prompts.q: What is an insulinoma and what is Whipple's triad?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: recurrent fasting hypos in a non-diabetic who is gaining weight.

points.p: Insulinoma: functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour secreting insulin
points.why: Weight gain from eating to prevent attacks is a clue.

points.p: Symptoms of hypoglycaemia
points.why: First part of the triad.

points.p: Low plasma glucose at the time of symptoms
points.why: The glucose must be measured during the episode.

points.p: Symptoms resolve after glucose is given
points.why: Third part of the triad.

prompts.q: How do you tell hypoglycaemia from DKA, HHS and stroke in a confused diabetic?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the glucose and the skin give it away before anything else.

points.p: Hypo: glucose below 4, sweaty, onset over minutes
points.why: DKA and HHS patients are dry and dehydrated.

points.p: DKA: high glucose, ketones, acidosis, type 1
points.why: Follows missed insulin or infection.

points.p: HHS: very high glucose, severe dehydration, days, type 2
points.why: Builds over days, not minutes.

points.p: Stroke mimic: always check glucose before calling a stroke
points.why: Hypoglycaemia can cause focal signs.

prompts.q: What is the first test for hypoglycaemia, and what confirms it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'initial investigation' in a confused insulin user is the finger-prick.

points.p: Capillary (finger-prick) blood glucose
points.why: Quick and changes management at once.

points.p: Laboratory blood glucose for confirmation
points.why: Send it without delaying treatment.

prompts.q: How does C-peptide separate the causes, and how is insulinoma diagnosed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: high insulin plus low C-peptide means a syringe.

points.p: Raised C-peptide: endogenous insulin (insulinoma or sulphonylurea)
points.why: A sulphonylurea screen separates these two.

points.p: Low C-peptide: exogenous (injected) insulin
points.why: Think of a healthcare worker or a relative's insulin.

points.p: Insulinoma: 72-hour supervised fast
points.why: Hormone profile (insulin, proinsulin, ketones) taken at the moment of the hypo.

prompts.q: How do you treat hypoglycaemia at each level of consciousness?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: GCS and IV access decide the route.

points.p: Conscious and can swallow: oral fast-acting glucose (tablets, Lucozade, juice)
points.why: First-line.

points.p: Conscious, cannot self-treat: buccal Glucogel
points.why: One tube.

points.p: GCS below 15 or seizing: IV glucose, 200 ml 10% or 100 ml 20% over 10 min
points.why: Over about 10 minutes.

points.p: No IV access: IM glucagon
points.why: Works less well when glycogen stores are low.

points.p: Then a longer-acting carbohydrate
points.why: Stops the glucose falling again.

prompts.q: What follow-up and driving advice does a patient need after a severe hypo?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: count the severe episodes and check whether one was at the wheel.

points.p: Medication review and diet review to find the cause
points.why: Stop or reduce the sulphonylurea; check renal function.

points.p: More than one severe episode while awake: stop driving, inform DVLA
points.why: Severe means needing help from another person.

points.p: One severe episode while driving: stop driving, inform DVLA
points.why: A single episode at the wheel is enough.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: symptoms decide between feeding and the neonatal unit.

points.p: Asymptomatic: encourage normal feeds and monitor
points.why: Most mild cases settle with feeding.

points.p: Symptomatic or very low: admit to neonatal unit for IV 10% dextrose
points.why: Jitteriness, poor feeding or seizures are symptoms.

prompts.q: Why do autonomic symptoms come first, and why can awareness be lost?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the order of symptoms and what blunts it.

points.p: Falling glucose triggers a sympathetic counter-regulatory response (adrenaline)
points.why: This is the warning sign.

points.p: The brain depends on glucose as its main fuel, so it fails next
points.why: Causes confusion, seizures, coma.

points.p: Repeated hypos and autonomic neuropathy blunt the warning response
points.why: Unheralded severe hypos follow.

prompts.q: How do insulin and sulphonylureas cause hypoglycaemia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: both work through insulin; one is injected, one is released.

points.p: Insulin drives glucose into cells
points.why: Mainly muscle and fat.

points.p: Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output
points.why: So fasting glucose cannot be maintained.

points.p: Sulphonylureas stimulate endogenous insulin release (close beta-cell K-ATP channels)
points.why: Regardless of glucose level, hence hypos with missed meals.

glossary.hypoglycaemia: Blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L causing autonomic and neuroglycopenic symptoms.
glossary.neuroglycopenic: Symptoms caused by the brain lacking glucose, such as confusion, drowsiness and seizures.
glossary.autonomic: Symptoms from the sympathetic nervous system: sweating, tremor, palpitations and anxiety.
glossary.counter-regulatory: Hormone responses (adrenaline, glucagon, cortisol) that raise glucose when it falls.
glossary.sulphonylurea: Oral diabetes drug class, such as gliclazide, that makes the pancreas release insulin.
glossary.gliclazide: A sulphonylurea; a common cause of hypoglycaemia, especially in kidney impairment.
glossary.metformin: First-line type 2 diabetes drug that lowers liver glucose output; rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone.
glossary.insulinoma: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour that secretes insulin and causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
glossary.Whipple's triad: Hypoglycaemic symptoms, a low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is given.
glossary.neuroendocrine tumour: A tumour of hormone-producing cells, which can secrete active hormones such as insulin.
glossary.C-peptide: Fragment cut from proinsulin when the body makes insulin; absent from injected insulin.
glossary.proinsulin: The precursor molecule that is split into insulin and C-peptide in beta cells.
glossary.exogenous: Coming from outside the body, such as injected insulin.
glossary.72-hour supervised fast: Diagnostic test for insulinoma: fasting in hospital with bloods taken when glucose drops.
glossary.capillary blood glucose: Finger-prick glucose reading at the bedside.
glossary.CBG: Capillary blood glucose, the bedside finger-prick reading.
glossary.Glucogel: A glucose gel squeezed into the cheek (buccal) for conscious patients who cannot self-treat.
glossary.buccal: Given inside the cheek, absorbed through the lining of the mouth.
glossary.glucagon: Hormone that releases glucose from liver glycogen; given IM when there is no IV access.
glossary.dextrose: Another name for glucose in IV fluids.
glossary.impaired hypoglycaemia awareness: Loss of the warning autonomic symptoms, so hypos go straight to confusion or coma.
glossary.autonomic neuropathy: Damage to autonomic nerves, which can blunt the warning response to hypoglycaemia.
glossary.DVLA: Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, the UK body that must be told about severe hypos.
glossary.severe hypoglycaemia: A hypo where the person needs help from someone else to treat it.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, a score of conscious level from 3 to 15.
glossary.DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: high glucose, ketones and acidosis, usually in type 1 diabetes.
glossary.HHS: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: very high glucose and dehydration in type 2 diabetes, over days.
glossary.K-ATP channel: ATP-sensitive potassium channel on beta cells; closing it triggers insulin release.
glossary.beta cells: Insulin-producing cells in the pancreatic islets.
glossary.hepatic glucose output: Glucose released by the liver from glycogen and gluconeogenesis.
glossary.gluconeogenesis: Making new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, mainly in the liver.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid fall in kidney function.
glossary.eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, a measure of kidney function.
glossary.neonatal hypoglycaemia: Low blood glucose in a newborn; prematurity is a key risk factor.
glossary.Lucozade: A glucose drink used as oral fast-acting glucose.
